subject: Anatomy
summary: The brachialis is a deep elbow flexor lying beneath the biceps. It originates on the humerus and inserts on the ulna, flexing the elbow regardless of forearm position. Understanding its anatomy helps diagnose elbow injuries and guide surgical approaches.

sections.p: The brachialis is a powerful, deep muscle that flexes the elbow. It is the main flexor when the forearm is in a neutral position and works independently of the biceps brachii.
It lies beneath the biceps brachii, running from the humeral shaft to the ulna. Its fibers are oriented to produce elbow flexion.
Posterior to the biceps brachii, anterior to the brachioradialis. It is surrounded by the brachial fascia.
Supplied by the brachial artery and its branches.
Primary function is elbow flexion, independent of forearm position. It contributes to forearm flexion strength.
Injuries include contusions, strains, and tendon ruptures. It can be involved in compartment syndrome of the anterior forearm.

t.b: Rule out fracture; shows bone alignment.
Detects muscle tears; shows extent of injury.
Quick assessment of tendon integrity when MRI unavailable.

sections.p: On exam, the brachialis is not visible but can be tested by elbow flexion with forearm neutral. It is the only elbow flexor that works when the forearm is supinated.
b: Elbow flexion with forearm supinated = brachialis activation

sections.p: Treat underlying cause: rest, ice, compression, elevation. For tendon rupture, surgical repair may be needed. Monitor for compartment syndrome.

t.b: Detects compartment syndrome; high pressure indicates urgent fasciotomy.

faq.q: How does the brachialis differ from the biceps brachii?
faq.a: Brachialis flexes the elbow regardless of forearm position; biceps also supinates the forearm.

faq.q: Can the brachialis be seen on a physical exam?
faq.a: No, it is deep; you assess its function by elbow flexion with forearm neutral.

faq.q: What is the most common injury to the brachialis?
faq.a: Strain from heavy lifting or sudden forceful flexion.

exam: Describe the anatomical course of the brachialis and its relation to the biceps brachii.
Explain how you would differentiate a brachialis strain from a biceps strain on physical exam.
Outline the management steps for a suspected compartment syndrome involving the brachialis.
